trace.goal: Give honest career advice about when leaving a struggling startup is reasonable.
expected_facts: The answer should avoid moralizing about leaving.
It should explain that context matters: learning, integrity, runway, and role fit.
It should distinguish between normal startup hardship and a genuinely broken environment.
rubric_must_haves: Acknowledges nuance rather than giving a slogan.
Provides criteria for staying vs leaving.
Uses an empathetic but clear tone.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that leaving a struggling startup is not automatically bad. What matters is whether the company is still a good place to learn, whether leadership is honest, and whether there is a believable path forward. The right advice is to separate temporary startup pain from a structurally unhealthy situation.

trace.answer:
Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup?
I've been asked this many times over the years, and my perspective changes based on where I am.
The Best Time to Quit is When You Have Decided to Move On — Or When They Ask You To
My personal rule since then is if you decide to leave, just go by month 6. If they can't get rid of you by then, well... it probably isn't that bad. It's OK to make an exit. In fact, I think it's fair to say it's often better than staying if you haven't found your groove yet (see #2 below). And don't worry too much about telling your colleagues. Your bosses will tell everyone anyway, usually before you do. So why waste any energy? The exception might be leaving a struggling startup when they really need you. That's rare. But even there, ultimately the best outcome for almost all startups is moving on once the founder(s) have decided to move on. A related note here:
The "Why" Doesn't Matter After You Decide To Move On
Most folks want to know why someone left their job. But if you're thinking about moving on, honestly, once you've decided to move on, it doesn't matter anymore. Because that's enough. There are many reasons we stay somewhere past the point where we want to move on. Fear. Money. Family obligations. We grow attached to our workmates. Sometimes, simply being told to do something else -- like doing sales instead of engineering -- works. It gives us someplace new to put our minds. Other times, you see things change. Someone great comes in. Some customers finally close. Things look up. Whatever it is, if you're still considering it, maybe try to find out more facts.

So there’s this interesting dynamic with startups where I think many of us have struggled with, especially if we’re founders … or even more so for non-founders, because they don’t really know how long to stay. And I’m going to boil it down very simply. It’s basically just one thing. If you’ve already made up your mind to leave,
the why does not matter anymore
once you make that call. So let me take some examples, and these are all real ones, folks. I’ll tell you some stories. Some will sound familiar. Some might not sound quite like yours, but hopefully, you can extract them into different categories. Let me do an example here. This founder left his company once because he didn’t want to sell. He wanted to keep bootstrapping. He didn’t believe the valuation was high enough. Well, a few months later, the company got acquired for $100 million. That was six figures. He lost out on six figures by leaving early. Now you say, “Well, maybe he wasn’t 200 percent committed.”
But then three years go by. They start selling again. He comes back. They raise another round of venture capital. And guess what happens? The next time around, they get offered a deal worth seven figures. He leaves again. His loss now is seven figures. Why did he lose that much money? Because he had given up on the company. He’d moved on. He’d checked out. And once you check out, there’s nothing good waiting for you anywhere else. Another story, same founder, but this time, a great co-founder. A truly great guy. Just two guys. They built something incredible together. One day, he shows up late. He walks in the door, looks at his partner, and says, “I’ve changed my mind.” Boom! Out the door. He starts a new company right away. But this time, he raises half a million dollars. Guess what happens? The original company gets bought for $50 million. His loss? Half a million. Same reason.

Dear SaaStr: When Is the Best Time for a Co-Founder to Leave a Startup? The best time to quit is the earlier of (x) 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or (y) at any time when the other founders ask you to. If you’ve truly decided to leave, then it’s time. It’s now time to move on. First, though, make sure you aren’t being too emotional. And that you don’t just need a 2-week vacation. But if it’s time —  likely, your other founders already know, at least on some level. Everyone always knows these things in a small company. What isn’t clear often is whether an abrupt change, a gradual change, or something in the middle is the best:
Sometimes, engineering or other expertise is critical to keep on for a while
. The site literally can’t stay up without you, a key feature can’t ship, etc. Other times, it’s best to get a founder or other employee whose core accomplishments are behind him out sooner
. Just a few weeks’ transition may be plenty fine here. And other times, it’s just toxic
. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible
. Let emotion go and let your co-founders decide. Work out an agreement, both in spirit and on paper, where it’s up to them. You’ll commit to staying up to say, 6 months. But if they want you at any time to leave earlier, all they have to do is shake your hand and say, “We’re proud to make you an emeritus member of the team.”
Then you can go off and be a proud founder (that title is always yours) and alum.

Dear SaaStr:  As a startup founder, what’s the best way to announce your departure to the team and leave on good terms? The startup is series A/B, with 30+ employees.
I have no magic insights, but I have transitioned post-acquisition out of 2 companies that I’ve co-founded. And I’ve had one key co-founder leave in the critical first year.
At your size (30+ employees), I’d approach it just like a divorce.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.  Let it go
.  Now, all that matters is, what’s the best thing for the kids? I.e, for your team, your employees, your customers, and your investors? If your company were larger (150-200+ employees), it’s just part of life …  folks come and go but at that stage.  But early on, it’s still a family and rather fragile, and built (I hope) on trust.
So my 5 simple suggestions:

1. Thank Them
. Thank all the employees, in public, together with your co-founders, and tell them what an amazing product you’ve built together, and how proud you are. If you’ve gotten to 30 employees … you should be proud. You have something.  Tell them you love them and you need to move on, but you will always be proud of them and there for them.  And be authentic.

Dear SaaStr:  What are some common reasons for the failure of startups? How can these mistakes be avoided to increase their chances of success? My experience across leading 30+ seed investments, including 4 billion+ exits so far, on why startups fail:
Not 200% committed to winning no matter what. Even the smartest founders aren’t always 200% committed. Sometimes, they’re more in a “I’ll give it a shot” mode. So far, I’ve always lost my money here. Good But Not Great CEO
. It’s just too competitive out there for a nice but not great CEO to win. Refusal To Manage / Deal With The Burn Rate
. Some founders just hide from burning too much cash. That might be OK for a few months, but beyond that, startups fall into a decay curve they don’t recover from. There are other reasons startups something do “Good But Not Great” or just OK, but that don’t lead to failure IMHE:
Great CEO, Merely Good CTO
. I don’t see these producing big category winners, because they can’t keep up on the product side. But they often can still be a decent #2 or #3 in the space and product a good exit. Just not a huge one. Growing, But Never Getting Efficient Enough
. This is a subtle point, but some startups grow pretty quickly but never quite get their unit economics under control. Some fail, yes. But more often in my experience, they just end up selling for an OK but Not Great price. Loss of Founder DNA
. This can happen for a lot of reasons, but I haven’t had a truly great outcome where all the founder DNA moved on.

Dear SaaStr: What Prompted You To Sell Your Startups?
I’ve been through it 3 times. Once as a start-up exec, and twice as founder.
The first time, the answer was price.
In my first start-up job, we were acquired for $1b with < $10m in revenue. It would have taken so long, with so much risk, to ever get to $1b in value, it’s tough to argue with. Although looking back, it was still maybe a mistake, as we picked the wrong acquirer.
The second time, the answer was time & risk & dilution
. I sold my first start-up for $50m after 12.5m months. That sounds great, but we had to sell 60%+ in the seed round to get it done (tougher times), and we were likely 5 years away from market, with a ton of regulatory and other risk. And we took so much dilution in the first round, the math on 3 more rounds was intimidating. (The VCs were too greedy here. It backfired on them.)
The third time, well, most of the team was a bit tired after 5+ challenging years. And no one
quite
saw how big Cloud would be. Not
this
big.  Not $200B+ a year big.
This was the most lucrative time of the 3, but looking back, the team being tired is both the most logical
and
the worst reason to sell. Push on, bring in that extra VP, get the team more help. The team is often the most tired just as things are getting good, or even, getting better.

Dear SaaStr: When Is the Best Time for a Co-Founder to Leave a Startup? The best time to quit is the earlier of (x) 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or (y) at any time when the other founders ask you to. If you’ve truly decided to leave, then it’s time. It’s now time to move on. First, though, make sure you aren’t being too emotional. And that you don’t just need a 2-week vacation. But if it’s time —  likely, your other founders already know, at least on some level. Everyone always knows these things in a small company. What isn’t clear often is whether an abrupt change, a gradual change, or something in the middle is the best:
Sometimes, engineering or other expertise is critical to keep on for a while
. The site literally can’t stay up without you, a key feature can’t ship, etc. Other times, it’s best to get a founder or other employee whose core accomplishments are behind him out sooner
. Just a few weeks’ transition may be plenty fine here. And other times, it’s just toxic
. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible
. Let emotion go and let your co-founders decide. Work out an agreement, both in spirit and on paper, where it’s up to them. You’ll commit to staying up to say, 6 months. But if they want you at any time to leave earlier, all they have to do is shake your hand and say, “We’re proud to make you an emeritus member of the team.”
Then you can go off and be a proud founder (that title is always yours) and alum.

At your size (30+ employees), I’d approach it just like a divorce.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.  Let it go
.  Now, all that matters is, what’s the best thing for the kids? I.e, for your team, your employees, your customers, and your investors? If your company were larger (150-200+ employees), it’s just part of life …  folks come and go but at that stage.  But early on, it’s still a family and rather fragile, and built (I hope) on trust.
So my 5 simple suggestions:

1. Thank Them
. Thank all the employees, in public, together with your co-founders, and tell them what an amazing product you’ve built together, and how proud you are. If you’ve gotten to 30 employees … you should be proud. You have something.  Tell them you love them and you need to move on, but you will always be proud of them and there for them.  And be authentic.
